analyses.title: Extraction de tâches dans les e-mails : une approche fondée sur les rôles sémantiques
analyses.research_question: Can a semantic-role-based symbolic system detect and structure action and information requests in professional French emails so that the action predicate and participants such as agent, theme, recipient, and temporal context are explicitly represented?
analyses.methodology: The authors formulate email task extraction as semantic role labeling rather than message- or sentence-level classification. Their symbolic pipeline combines a VerbeNet-based module that maps dependency-derived syntactic frames to semantic roles with a second hand-written rule module intended to improve coverage when the lexical-semantic resource fails. Filters then distinguish action requests from information requests using morphosyntactic form, the Agent role, recipient identity, and semantic classes of governing predicates. Evaluation uses 1,000 development emails and 200 manually annotated professional French test emails, with precision, recall, and F-measure reported at message, request, and semantic-role levels, both before and after manual spelling correction.

key_findings.finding: The proposed representation structures a task around a predicate and semantic arguments such as Agent, Theme/Patient, Recipient, Time, Location, Purpose, Manner, Instrument, Cause, and Consequence, making it substantially closer to structured action-argument extraction than simple email classification.

On the uncorrected test emails, the system reports F1 scores of 0.91 for detecting messages containing requests, 0.83 for action requests, 0.93 for information requests, and 0.84 for semantic-role extraction.

After manual spelling correction, reported F1 rises to 0.94 for request-containing messages, 0.88 for action requests, 0.94 for information requests, and 0.89 for semantic roles, indicating notable sensitivity to noisy email text.

The action-request filter requires an Agent corresponding to the email recipient and uses imperative, semi-auxiliary, or complement-clause constructions while excluding predicates governed by conjectural verbs such as think, presume, hope, or believe.

The task definition explicitly allows negative requested actions and includes a Time semantic role, but the evaluation does not separately measure negation attachment or deadline-to-action attachment accuracy.
The test corpus contains only five Time-role annotations among 203 action-request role annotations, so evidence for robust deadline extraction is very limited.

Although the paper identifies implicit subjects as a weakness of prior pattern-based systems, it does not provide a dedicated evaluation of implicit or group assignee resolution; its action filter still depends on obtaining an Agent role that matches the recipient.

limitations: The evaluation is limited to 200 French professional emails, of which 87 contain at least one request.
Only 74 action requests occur in the test corpus, and temporal information is especially sparse with five Time-role annotations.
The paper does not report dedicated metrics for individual semantic roles, implicit assignees, group assignees, deadline-to-action relations, conditions, negation scope, or modality attachment.
The system is rule-heavy and depends on dependency parsing, named-entity recognition, VerbeNet coverage, manually developed rules, and manually added lexical-semantic coverage.
Manual spelling correction materially improves recall, highlighting sensitivity to authentic noisy email text.
The paper focuses on requests from the recipient's perspective rather than a general schema covering commitments, decisions, completed actions, or arbitrary enterprise-chat participants.
No public implementation is identified in the paper.
raw_claims: The paper treats task extraction as semantic-role annotation centered on an action predicate.
Its intended structured output answers questions such as who performs an action, what is acted on, for whom, and when.
The primary resource-based module maps dependency-derived syntactic frames to semantic frames from French VerbeNet.
A second rule-based module attempts to recover semantic roles that the resource-based module misses.
Action requests are filtered partly by requiring the Agent to correspond to the email recipient.
The authors explicitly include negative action requests in their task definition.
Time is one of the semantic roles considered relevant to email actions.
The development set contains 1,000 emails and the test set contains 200 emails.
The test set contains 74 action requests and 65 information requests.
Semantic-role F1 increases from 0.84 to 0.89 after manual spelling correction.

analyses.title: Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction with Contextualized Span Representations
analyses.research_question: Can a unified span-based information-extraction architecture combine contextualized language representations and dynamically propagated span graphs to improve entity, relation, and event extraction across domains?
analyses.methodology: DyGIE++ enumerates candidate within-sentence spans, represents them with multi-sentence BERT encodings, and optionally refines span representations through task-specific graph propagation for coreference, relations, and events. Shared representations feed neural scoring functions for named entities, relations, event triggers, and trigger-argument roles, with coreference used as an auxiliary task. The authors evaluate variants using BERT plus an LSTM or BERT fine-tuning on ACE05, SciERC, GENIA, and wet-lab-protocol data and compare them with previous state-of-the-art systems. Evaluation requires exact span matches for entities, relations, event triggers, and event arguments, with additional label correctness required for classification scores.

key_findings.finding: The framework achieves reported state-of-the-art results on the three high-level extraction tasks and on all listed subtasks except event argument identification, although event-argument gains are not statistically supported.

Coreference propagation improves named-entity recognition across the evaluated domains and improves relation extraction on SciERC, demonstrating that non-local mention links can improve span representations.
Event-specific graph propagation does not improve the best ACE event-extraction results; the authors hypothesize that asymmetric trigger-argument structure may require better higher-order modeling.
Increasing BERT's sentence context can help some entity, relation, trigger, and argument tasks, but the effects are task-dependent rather than uniformly positive.
key_findings.section: Section 4, Benefits of Cross-Sentence Context with BERT

key_findings.finding: Evaluation explicitly requires matching gold offsets, making this paper directly relevant to exact evidence-span extraction methodology.

For event extraction, candidate arguments are restricted to spans in the same sentence as the trigger, so the architecture as evaluated does not directly solve cross-sentence or cross-message action-argument attachment.
The ACE event preprocessing used in the paper ignores time and value arguments, limiting the reported event experiments for deadline-to-action extraction.

The datasets and schemas do not define workplace-specific assignee, group-assignee, deadline, condition, negation, or deontic-modality slots, so those capabilities are not established by the reported results.

limitations: None of the evaluated datasets is an authentic workplace email or enterprise-chat corpus.
Event arguments are modeled only within the trigger's sentence in the evaluated event task.
ACE preprocessing explicitly discards time and value arguments, which removes evidence needed for deadline-oriented evaluation.
The task schemas do not directly represent implicit assignees, group responsibility, conditions, negation scope, or obligation/permission modality.
The strongest event argument identification result is below the cited previous state of the art, and averaged event-argument results do not demonstrate improvement.
Some headline results use the best single run, while the appendix shows materially different averages across random seeds.
Exact span matching is evaluated, but the evidence spans are benchmark entity/event arguments rather than workplace action or decision evidence.
raw_claims: DyGIE++ jointly models named entities, relations, event triggers, event arguments, and auxiliary coreference links.
Candidate spans are enumerated only within sentence boundaries.
BERT is supplied with surrounding-sentence context through a sliding-window scheme.
Dynamic graph updates can propagate information through predicted coreference, relation, or event links.
Event argument candidates are predicted entity mentions in the same sentence as the event trigger.
Entity and relation correctness requires exact matching of gold spans.
Event trigger correctness also depends on matching gold offsets.
Coreference propagation is especially beneficial on SciERC, where long-range coreference and abbreviations are common.
The best event extraction configuration does not benefit from event propagation.
ACE event preprocessing in these experiments excludes time and value arguments.
The authors publicly released the DyGIE++ implementation.

analyses.title: Decision Detection Using Hierarchical Graphical Models
analyses.research_question: Can hierarchical graphical models improve automatic detection of decision-discussion regions in multi-party meetings by jointly modeling observable utterance features, decision dialogue acts, and higher-level decision regions?
analyses.methodology: The study uses 17 scenario-driven meetings from the AMI Meeting Corpus and manually annotated transcripts containing decision dialogue acts for issues, resolution proposals, resolution restatements, and agreements. The proposed three-level hierarchical graphical model represents observable utterance, dialogue-act, and prosodic features at the bottom level, decision dialogue acts at the middle level, and decision-region membership at the top level. Decision regions are evaluated in 30-second windows, with model structure and thresholds selected experimentally. The HGM is compared with a hierarchical SVM approach and a rule-based classifier using directed graphical-model outputs under 17-fold cross-validation on the same data.

key_findings.finding: The hierarchical graphical model reports precision 0.69, recall 0.96, and F1 0.80 for decision-region detection, compared with F1 0.55 for the DGM method and 0.50 for the hierarchical SVM in the paper's controlled comparison.

The improvement is attributed to jointly modeling dependencies between high-level decision regions, mid-level decision dialogue acts, and observable utterance features rather than detecting decision-related utterances independently.

The annotation scheme distinguishes issue, resolution proposal, resolution restatement, and agreement utterances, thereby representing stages of collective decision formation rather than only a binary decision/non-decision label.
An utterance can belong to more than one decision-dialogue-act class, and multiple utterances of the same class can contribute to one decision discussion.

The experiment relies on manual transcripts and manually annotated dialogue-act information; it therefore does not establish equivalent performance on raw enterprise chat or automatically transcribed meetings.

The model detects temporal regions of decision discussion but does not extract structured decision arguments such as the chosen proposition, responsible assignee, deadline, condition, negation, modality, or exact supporting evidence spans.

limitations: Only 17 scenario-driven AMI meetings are used, with four participants playing predefined design-team roles.
Experiments use manual transcripts rather than noisy ASR output or authentic enterprise text chat.
Dialogue-act annotations used as features are manually supplied in the reported experiments.
Evaluation is performed on 30-second decision-region windows rather than exact token or phrase evidence spans.
The output schema identifies decision regions and DDA types but not structured decision propositions, action owners, group assignees, deadlines, conditions, negation, or modality.
The model structure and decision threshold are hand selected or hand tuned.
No released implementation of the authors' HGM system is identified in the paper.
raw_claims: The experiments use 17 meetings from the AMI Meeting Corpus.
The meetings are scenario-driven design-team discussions involving four participant roles.
The decision annotation distinguishes issues, resolution proposals, resolution restatements, and agreements.
The manual transcripts contain 15,680 utterances.
Decision dialogue acts constitute a sparse minority of all utterances.
A three-level HGM connects observable features, decision dialogue acts, and decision-region variables.
Decision-region accuracy is evaluated using 30-second windows.
The reported HGM F1 for decision-region detection is 0.80.
The corresponding DGM and SVM F1 scores are 0.55 and 0.50.
The paper does not produce a structured record of the arguments of each detected decision.

analyses.title: Event Time Extraction with a Decision Tree of Neural Classifiers
analyses.research_question: Can a hierarchical decision tree of neural classifiers use document-wide temporal evidence to anchor events to precise single-day or multi-day time intervals more accurately than local temporal-relation systems?
analyses.methodology: The system decomposes event-time extraction into a decision tree whose local classifiers determine event duration type, relation to document creation time, relevant temporal expressions, temporal relations, and begin or end points. Most tree nodes use convolutional neural classifiers over word embeddings, position features, and the text between an event and a temporal expression, while a narrowing stage is rule based. Unlike systems limited to nearby temporal links, all event-temporal-expression pairs in a document can be considered. The model is evaluated on the TimeBank-EventTime Corpus with strict and relaxed accuracy, repeated over 25 random seeds, and is additionally applied without retraining to SemEval-2015 Task 4 timeline generation.

key_findings.finding: Document-wide temporal reasoning is empirically important because the paper reports that a substantial fraction of events require temporal evidence outside the same or adjacent sentence to recover their occurrence time.
The full system achieves 42.0% strict overall accuracy against 56.7% inter-annotator agreement, while relaxed overall accuracy is 84.6%.
For single-day events the model reaches 74.6% exact-match accuracy, a reported 33.1 percentage-point improvement over CAEVO in the paper's conclusion.
Multi-day anchoring remains much harder, with 24.5% strict accuracy and particularly low 28.5% strict accuracy for begin-point extraction.

Removing the text between an event and its temporal expression reduces overall strict accuracy by 9.7 percentage points, supporting explicit modeling of the linguistic relation connecting a time expression to an event.

The architecture explicitly predicts whether a relevant temporal expression is BEFORE, AFTER, or otherwise related to an event, which is methodologically applicable to deadline-to-action attachment even though deadlines and workplace actions are not the paper's target schema.
The system cannot create dates that must be inferred but are not explicitly represented by a temporal expression in the document; such out-of-document dates affect 12.6% of test labels.
Applied without retraining to SemEval-2015 timeline generation, the system obtains total F1 32.59 versus 28.58 for the cited previous best system, a difference of 4.01 points.

limitations: The corpus consists of news articles and broadcast transcripts rather than workplace email or enterprise chat.
The method anchors generic events, not task requests, decisions, assignees, commitments, or deadlines as distinct workplace concepts.
It does not model deontic modality, action negation, conditions, or group/implicit responsibility.
Temporal expressions are assumed to have already been detected and normalized by another component.
Decision-tree errors propagate from early classifiers to later temporal decisions.
The training data are small; the paper notes only 22 training documents when discussing neural-model limitations.
The system cannot synthesize required out-of-document dates, which affect 12.6% of the evaluated labels.
Multi-day event begin-point extraction remains substantially below human agreement.
raw_claims: The system decomposes event-time anchoring into a sequence of local classification decisions.
Most local classifiers are convolutional neural networks and one narrowing stage is rule based.
The model can compare an event with temporal expressions anywhere in the document.
The TimeBank-EventTime annotations distinguish single-day events from events spanning multiple days.
Multi-day events receive separate begin-point and end-point annotations.
The system reports 42.0% strict overall accuracy.
Single-day exact-match accuracy is 74.6%.
Multi-day strict accuracy is 24.5%.
Removing intervening-text features lowers strict accuracy by 9.7 percentage points.
Out-of-document dates account for 12.6% of test labels and cannot be generated by the system.
The authors evaluate 25 random-seed runs rather than reporting a single neural training run.
The implementation is publicly released.

analyses.title: Focused Meeting Summarization via Unsupervised Relation Extraction
analyses.research_question: Can unsupervised relation extraction identify the salient content phrases associated with individual meeting decisions well enough to support focused, potentially abstractive decision summaries?
analyses.methodology: The authors recast focused decision summarization as unsupervised relation extraction, representing latent relations as indicator-argument pairs in clusters of decision-related dialogue acts. A generative relation-learning model is adapted using posterior regularization with syntactic, prevalence, occurrence, and discourse constraints, together with lexical, syntactic, speaker, dialogue-act, adjacency-pair, topic, and WordNet-derived features. The method is evaluated on the AMI Meeting Corpus using both gold decision-related-dialogue-act clusterings and automatically produced clusterings. Human-written decision abstracts are the gold summaries, and systems are compared with utterance baselines, a generic unsupervised relation extractor, supervised SVM and CRF systems, and an extractive upper bound using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-SU4.

key_findings.finding: The paper distinguishes a Decision Cue from the Decision Content and argues that only the content phrase, rather than the entire decision-related utterance, should normally enter a focused decision summary.
The relation representation extracts phrase-level indicator-argument structures, providing finer evidence than whole-utterance decision detection and preserving identifiable source phrases.

Under gold decision clusterings, configurations of the unsupervised method outperform the reported utterance-level and generic relation-extraction baselines on ROUGE-1 F1 and ROUGE-SU4 F1, while remaining competitive rather than superior to the strongest supervised SVM.
With true clusterings, the 10-relation model reports ROUGE-1 F1 of 37.47, ROUGE-2 F1 of 12.20, and ROUGE-SU4 F1 of 14.59; the supervised SVM reports 40.87, 12.91, and 16.29 respectively.
Performance falls substantially when automatically produced decision clusterings replace gold clusterings, showing strong dependence on accurate upstream association of dialogue acts with decisions.

Learned decision cues include group-oriented expressions involving 'we', including wrap-up, suggestion, and final-decision patterns, but these are discourse cues rather than explicit structured group-assignee annotations.
The model does not generate a complete abstractive decision sentence; it identifies content phrases intended to support later generation.
Gold supervision is available for decision-related utterances and human abstracts, not for a workplace argument schema containing assignee, action, deadline, condition, negation, or modality spans.

limitations: The experiments use scenario-driven AMI meetings rather than authentic workplace email or enterprise chat.
The system assumes that decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified and grouped, or relies on an upstream clustering system whose errors substantially reduce performance.
The extracted relation arguments are designed for summary content, not for normalized structured slots such as decision proposition, assignee, action, deadline, condition, negation, or modality.
Group expressions such as 'we' are learned as decision cues but are not resolved to concrete group membership or responsibility.
There is no explicit gold annotation or metric for exact evidence-span boundaries of the extracted indicator and argument phrases.
ROUGE against human decision abstracts evaluates lexical summary overlap rather than factual argument attachment accuracy.
The method identifies phrases for later abstraction but does not itself produce a final abstractive summary.
No public implementation is identified in the paper.
raw_claims: The method treats focused decision summarization as an unsupervised relation-extraction problem.
A decision-related utterance may contain discourse cue material that should not appear in the final decision summary.
The desired decision content is modeled as an argument phrase associated with a lexical indicator.
Posterior regularization introduces syntactic, prevalence, occurrence, and discourse constraints.
One discourse constraint encourages relation instances near the end of a decision discussion.
The feature set includes dialogue-act type, speaker role, topic, adjacency-pair structure, syntax, and WordNet information.
The experiments use the AMI corpus, which contains manually written abstracts for individual decisions.
The paper evaluates both perfect decision-related-dialogue-act clusterings and automatically generated clusterings.
Automatic clustering causes a large reduction in ROUGE scores for all evaluated systems.
Group expressions using 'we' appear among learned decision-cue patterns.
The proposed method outputs phrase-based relations rather than a complete generated decision abstract.
